demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Samir was seventy-seven when the incident occurred at the university environmental research center where he had spent four decades calibrating sampling equipment and studying soil degradation. He was adjusting a pressurized core cylinder when a colleague stepped beside him to share the weight of a heavy sediment tray. Samir felt a quiet satisfaction in the shared task, his shoulders dropping as he allowed himself to relax. A moment later, the colleague reached around him in a warm, lingering hug, and Samir smiled, feeling unguarded. Then came the sharp hiss and the crash. The glass cylinder had failed, and a jagged shard had sliced deeply into the colleague's forearm. Samir stood frozen, his own chest heaving as he watched the blood pool on the sterile tile floor. He knew the injury would heal, but the responsibility had lodged in him. In the weeks that followed, Samir found that remembering the event did not feel like recalling a past occurrence. When the memory surfaced, it was not a distant story but a sudden relocation into the lab. The glass shattering seemed to echo in his ears, and he would catch himself reaching out to steady equipment that was no longer moving. What frightened him most was the sheer extremity of it; the memory felt so disproportionate, so extreme, that he would pause mid-sentence and wonder if the entire thing had actually happened to him or belonged to someone else. He knew exactly what had occurred, but when he tried to explain it to his wife, Leila, the words would gather at the back of his throat, refusing to form. He could trace the arc of the accident in his mind, yet the precise details remained locked behind a quiet barrier of meaning, leaving him with a heavy certainty that he could not articulate. Over the months, the lab itself became a landscape of subtle alarms. Samir began to notice the sound of heavy breathing everywhere-the rapid exhalations of technicians moving between spectrometers, the labored sighs of visitors, even the steady breath of the laboratory itself growing taut in his attention. Each time a sound thickened like a drawn breath, his pulse would quicken, and he would instinctively step back from the equipment he had once handled without hesitation. He came to believe that relaxation carried its own weight. When he allowed himself to feel happy or unburdened, a low-grade vigilance would settle in his chest, as though his body were bracing for the moment the glass would give way again. At home, Leila's affection became both a comfort and a trigger. When she reached up to adjust his collar or pressed her cheek to his shoulder, Samir would stiffen, certain that the contact might pull him into the same unguarded moment that had preceded the injury. He did not withdraw from her, but he learned to lean forward just enough to keep her embrace at a measured distance. The avoidance strategies accumulated quietly but reshaped his days. He delegated the heavier core samples to junior researchers, citing a need for fresh eyes, though he was really keeping the pressurized vessels at arm's length. In staff meetings, when laughter rose and shoulders relaxed, Samir would remain still, conserving his breath, until the moment passed. His meticulous approach to the environment remained intact, but the physical rhythm of his work had slowed; he walked more deliberately, spoke more carefully, and measured every interaction as though weighing potential consequences. At seventy-eight, Samir sought help not because the memories had grown worse, but because the quiet certainty that had settled over him was beginning to narrow his world. He was tired of carrying the weight of a story that felt too large for his own body, and he hoped that someone could help him find the words to hold it, so that he might finally allow himself to relax without fearing the sound of his own breath.
